title: New Scientist Story Ideas — Schizophrenia — October 2026

studies.title: Most people have intrusive fears of "going crazy" — and OCD makes them stick
studies.journal: Journal of Behavior Therapy and Experimental Psychiatry
studies.ns_score_reason: vividly relatable and the first prevalence estimate for a fear patient communities already talk about, but it is a student analogue sample, not a clinical one.
studies.the_study: Researchers at Memorial University of Newfoundland surveyed 154 university students about unwanted intrusive thoughts and compulsions centered on the fear of becoming psychotic — informally known as "schizophrenia OCD". Some 83 percent reported at least one such thought or behavior in their lifetime; the most common intrusion was fear of losing control of your thoughts or actions (50.6 percent), while fear of actually developing a psychotic illness (18.3 percent) was rated the most distressing. Health anxiety and negative beliefs about losing control predicted these fears over and above overall OCD severity.
studies.why_it_matters: It suggests that fearing you are going mad is close to a universal human experience rather than a rare symptom, and that what turns it into a clinical problem is not the thought itself but what you believe losing control would mean.
studies.pitch_angle: Open on the 2am thought almost everyone has had — *what if I'm losing my mind?* — and the finding that four in five young adults have had it, complete with the quiet rituals (half the sample "replaced bad thoughts with better ones") they use to make it go away. The hook is that the content of the obsession is near-universal; the pathology lies in the meaning assigned to it. Call Emily Fawcett's group at Memorial University, and ask an OCD clinician why this subtype goes unrecognized in standard checklists dominated by contamination and symmetry.
studies.wider_angle: A feature for a health or culture outlet on how psychiatric diagnoses leak into lay anxiety — people with OCD now obsess about having schizophrenia, people with health anxiety google dementia symptoms. How does public mental-health literacy create new obsessional content? Fits a long-read in a general-interest magazine.
studies.caveats: Non-clinical student sample (N=154) with self-reported measures and OCD defined by cut-off scores, not diagnostic interview; cross-sectional, so no evidence on what comes first; population unlikely to generalize beyond young, educated adults.

studies.title: People in early psychosis say romance is central to recovery — their clinics almost never ask
studies.ns_score_reason: a genuine blind spot in psychosis care told in patients' own words, though qualitative work with 20 people can only describe, not quantify.
studies.the_study: Researchers at Queen's University conducted in-depth interviews with 20 people attending early psychosis intervention programs in Ontario, Canada, and analyzed them using reflexive thematic analysis. Participants described intimacy, romance and sexuality as both a goal of recovery and a yardstick for measuring it — yet reported that clinicians rarely raised the subject, and when they did, it often came with stipulations or warnings. Participants also described stigma, symptom interference, lost relationships and narrowed opportunities as the main barriers.
studies.why_it_matters: Services built around symptom reduction may be ignoring the outcome patients themselves use to judge whether they are getting better, which has direct implications for how recovery is defined and measured.
studies.pitch_angle: Lead on the mismatch — clinicians track voices and medication adherence; patients track whether anyone will date them. Open on a participant describing being told relationships were something to postpone until they were "stable". The surprise is that a dimension clinicians treat as a risk to be managed is the one patients treat as the measure of recovery. Call Christopher Bowie at Queen's University; worth also approaching an early-intervention service lead on why the topic is avoided.
studies.wider_angle: A reported piece for a health-policy or disability-focused outlet on sexual citizenship in mental health care — who gets to be assumed capable of consent, desire and parenthood, and how capacity assessments and institutional risk-aversion shape that. Different story, broader stakes.
studies.caveats: Small qualitative sample (N=20), single region and service model, self-report by design, no quantitative outcome data; findings are exploratory and describe experiences rather than testing an intervention.

studies.title: Women's verbal memory advantage vanishes after a first episode of psychosis
studies.journal: Spanish Journal of Psychiatry and Mental Health
studies.ns_score_reason: a tidy sex-by-genotype interaction in a decent family-based cohort, but single-SNP findings need replication and the functional story is admittedly speculative.
studies.the_study: A Spanish team genotyped 486 people — patients with first-episode psychosis, their unaffected siblings and controls — and tested them on the Rey Auditory Verbal Learning Test. Among controls and siblings, women carrying the C allele of rs9896243 (in the NSF gene) outperformed men on immediate, short-delay and long-delay recall. In patients with first-episode psychosis, that female advantage disappeared entirely, and male patients carrying the C allele showed the most pronounced recognition deficits.
studies.why_it_matters: It is early evidence that a genetic variant's effect on memory is not fixed but depends on both sex and illness state — which would complicate the common assumption that cognitive risk genes act the same way in everyone.
studies.pitch_angle: Start with the well-replicated observation that women with schizophrenia tend to have better verbal memory than men, then the twist: in this cohort the female advantage was present in healthy relatives but gone in patients, and the same allele that helped women appeared to hurt men with psychosis. The hook is a gene whose effect flips sign depending on who carries it. Call Rosa Ayesa-Arriola at IDIVAL in Santander, who runs the first-episode cohort.
studies.wider_angle: A broader feature for a science or medicine outlet on sex-stratified psychiatric genetics — why most risk-gene studies pool men and women, what gets lost, and whether sex-informed polygenic scores are coming. Fits a specialist genomics or precision-medicine publication.
studies.caveats: Observational and cross-sectional (no causal inference); single candidate SNP in a modest cohort, needs independent replication; functional annotation is explicitly described by the authors as hypothesis-generating; single-center Spanish sample.

studies.title: Genetic evidence points to clozapine itself driving diabetes risk
studies.journal: The World Journal of Biological Psychiatry
studies.ns_score_reason: Mendelian randomization lends causal weight to a long-standing clinical worry, but the biomarker list is a hypothesis-generating pipeline, not a validated test.
studies.the_study: An Adelaide-based team used Mendelian randomization — exploiting genetic variants that influence how fast people metabolize clozapine — to probe whether the drug causes cardiometabolic harm rather than merely accompanying it. Higher genetically-predicted plasma clozapine levels and a higher clozapine-norclozapine ratio were associated with increased risk of type 2 diabetes and higher blood pressure. A phenome-scan-colocalization-MR pipeline flagged 28 markers tied to clozapine metabolism loci, 16 of which showed associations with cardiometabolic outcomes, including hematological and excretory traits.
studies.why_it_matters: Clozapine remains the only drug that works for many people with treatment-resistant schizophrenia, and the possibility of identifying in advance who will suffer metabolic harm would change a brutal risk-benefit calculation for hundreds of thousands of patients.
studies.pitch_angle: Open on the trade-off a psychiatrist makes every time they start clozapine: the most effective antipsychotic we have, and the one most likely to give you diabetes. The news is that genetic instruments — not just correlational patient records — now point toward drug exposure itself, and toward blood markers that might flag vulnerable patients before weight gain starts. Call Dan Stacey or Scott Clark at Adelaide University. Avoid implying anyone should change their dose: the authors explicitly say prospective validation is missing.
studies.wider_angle: A feature for a pharmacology or health-systems outlet on why clozapine is simultaneously underprescribed (because of mandatory blood monitoring) and dangerous, and whether predictive genotyping could unlock access for patients currently denied it. Fits a medicine-focused trade or policy publication.
studies.caveats: Genetic-epidemiological inference, not a clinical trial; authors state findings do not establish causation without prospective validation; relies on existing GWAS summary data whose ancestry composition limits generalizability; no patient-level outcomes.

studies.title: There may be no single recipe for recovering from schizophrenia
studies.ns_score_reason: a neat explanation for why the recovery literature keeps contradicting itself, limited by a small single-country sample.
studies.the_study: Japanese researchers assessed 101 people with schizophrenia or schizoaffective disorder on symptoms, depression, cognition, social functioning and metacognition, then used finite mixture regression to test whether a single model of "personal recovery" fits everyone. It does not: the analysis found distinct latent classes with different association structures. In one, recovery tracked social functioning, depression, positive symptoms and metacognition; in another — with comparable symptom and functioning levels — no dominant predictor emerged at all. Negative symptoms mattered in both.
studies.why_it_matters: It offers a concrete statistical reason why studies of what helps people recover from psychosis keep disagreeing — the field may have been averaging across groups for whom recovery works in fundamentally different ways.
studies.pitch_angle: Lead with the problem readers can feel: two people with the same diagnosis, the same symptom scores and the same level of functioning, for whom completely different things determine whether life feels worth living. The hook is a methodological result with a human payoff — "average patient" models may be an artifact. Call Hiroki Okada at Hyogo Medical University, and get a rehabilitation clinician's view on whether services can realistically individualize.
studies.wider_angle: A broader piece for a statistics-literate or health-research outlet on the quiet crisis of averaging in psychology and medicine — ergodicity, mixture models, and why group-level findings so often fail the individual in front of you. Fits a data-science or research-methods publication.
studies.caveats: Small sample (N=101) for a latent-class method that is data-hungry; cross-sectional and observational, so classes are associative rather than causal; one of the three classes too small to interpret; single-country sample with a specific rehabilitation service context.

studies.title: Two ways reality can go wrong: the philosopher's case for comparing borderline and schizophrenia
studies.ns_score_reason: a genuinely arresting idea about what the world feels like in two very different conditions, but it is conceptual scholarship with no new data.
studies.the_study: Two phenomenologists contrast the lived experience of borderline personality disorder with that of schizophrenia, arguing that both involve a disturbed relationship to reality but in opposite directions. Schizophrenia, they argue, is marked by an "evanescence of reality" — the world thins out and the person searches obliquely for hidden meaning — whereas borderline experience, especially in acute distress, involves an "excess of reality": encounters, bodily sensations and perceptions arrive as raw, abrasive, inescapable fact. They describe this as "ontic gravity", a crushing inability to step back from what is immediately given.
studies.why_it_matters: Not much changes clinically yet, but it reframes "derealization" — usually treated as one symptom — as potentially two opposite failures of the same system, and gives a vocabulary to an experience patients often struggle to describe.
studies.pitch_angle: Open on what it means to be unable to take anything with a pinch of salt — to have every comment, ache and glance land as unmediated fact. The surprise is the inversion: we assume psychiatric distress means losing touch with reality, but one condition may involve too much contact with it. Call Giovanni Stanghellini, and pair him with a clinician who works with both diagnoses to test whether patients recognize the description. Be explicit that this is theory, not a finding.
studies.wider_angle: A philosophy-of-mind feature for a literary or ideas outlet on the revival of phenomenological psychiatry — Husserl's epoché repurposed as a clinical tool, and whether first-person description can earn a place next to biomarkers in a field dominated by neuroimaging and genomics.
studies.caveats: Conceptual/theoretical paper with no participants, no data and no empirical test; claims are not falsified or quantified here; the comparison risks essentializing two heterogeneous diagnostic categories.

trends_raw:
**Convergent findings**
- **The "average patient" problem keeps surfacing, now in recovery research.** Last run's psychometric reassurance ("Computational models of memory turn out to be as reliable as the simple scores they replace", PMID 42765980) and the negative EEG result where group separation failed to identify individuals (PMID 41124326) framed the gap between describing groups and describing people. The new "There may be no single recipe for recovering from schizophrenia" (PMID 42734987) attacks the same gap from the other side: fit a mixture model and the single "predictors of personal recovery" equation dissolves into classes with different association structures.
- **Phenomenology continues its run.** Last run carried self-disturbance as a mediator from childhood neglect to psychotic experiences (PMID 42740395) and voice hearers negotiating autonomy rather than simply losing it (PMID 41354941). "Two ways reality can go wrong" (PMID 42853770) is the theoretical companion piece, proposing an "evanescence of reality" in schizophrenia against an "excess of reality" in borderline personality disorder — the same intellectual revival, now arguing at the level of concepts rather than questionnaires.

**Advances**
- **Clozapine's metabolic harm moves from management to causal attribution.** Last run compared counter-measures in real-world care ("Metformin, but not the standard add-on drug, curbs weight gain in people taking clozapine", PMID 42742489) and described a disturbed gut community in clozapine-treated patients with no unmedicated comparator (PMID 42758012). "Genetic evidence points to clozapine itself driving diabetes risk" (PMID 42472444) uses Mendelian randomization to argue the exposure itself — not the illness or lifestyle it travels with — raises type 2 diabetes risk and blood pressure, and flags candidate markers for identifying vulnerable patients in advance.
- **Cognition in genetic risk gains a sex dimension.** The 22q11.2 consortium study (PMID 42765380) found a consistently shaped cognitive profile with no domain-specific signature in those who developed psychosis. "Women's verbal memory advantage vanishes after a first episode of psychosis" (PMID 42843653) adds a moderator that pooled analyses would erase: an NSF-gene allele associated with better verbal recall in women among controls and siblings, with that advantage absent in patients and male carriers showing the worst recognition deficits.

**New themes**
- **Patient-defined recovery outcomes.** "People in early psychosis say romance is central to recovery — their clinics almost never ask" (PMID 41891676) is the first item in this topic memory on intimacy and sexuality as an outcome domain, and sits naturally alongside last run's voice-hearing work (PMID 41354941) on meaning rather than symptom suppression.
- **Psychiatric vocabulary as obsessional content.** "Most people have intrusive fears of 'going crazy' — and OCD makes them stick" (PMID 42800306) is new territory for this topic: schizophrenia as an object of public fear rather than a clinical population, with 83 percent of a student sample reporting lifetime intrusions about losing their mind.
feature_pitch_raw:
**The pattern:** Four studies in this batch converge on the subjective life of psychosis as something services neither measure nor ask about. People in early psychosis programs use intimacy and romance as their yardstick for recovery while clinicians avoid the topic (PMID 41891676); a mixture-model analysis shows that what predicts personal recovery differs fundamentally between patients with identical symptom and functioning scores (PMID 42734987); phenomenologists argue that "derealization" may be two opposite failures, a thinning of reality in schizophrenia versus a crushing excess of it in borderline states (PMID 42853770); and the fear of going mad turns out to be close to universal in the general population, with the pathology lying in what people believe losing control would mean (PMID 42800306).

**Why pitch this now:** Services are being rebuilt around "personal recovery" as a stated goal at the same moment the evidence suggests there is no single thing that drives it and no routine way to ask about the outcomes patients actually care about — a gap that is about to be inherited by outcome-based commissioning and app-based symptom tracking.

**Angle:** A reported feature on what recovery from psychosis means to the people in it, built from patient accounts and set against the symptom scales, remission criteria and averaged regression models that define success on the clinical side — for a general readership that assumes psychiatric improvement means fewer voices.

**Potential headlines:**
- What people with psychosis count as getting better, and what their clinics count instead
- Two patients, the same symptom scores, and nothing in common about what helps them
- The questions nobody asks you after a first episode of psychosis

**Potential outlets:**
- **New Scientist Mind** — the mixture-model result and the intimacy interviews give a familiar "recovery" story a concrete, evidence-led spine rather than a human-interest one.
- **The Guardian** science/health desk — strong record on service-user voices in mental health care and on what services decline to discuss, including sexuality and risk aversion.
- **Aeon** — the phenomenology strand, thinned versus excessive reality, is exactly their register, and the recovery-measurement material keeps it grounded.
- **STAT** — the outcome-measurement angle, what early intervention programs count as success and why, fits their coverage of how care is evaluated and paid for.

# Fact-Check Report: New Scientist Story Ideas — Schizophrenia — October 2026
**Checked:** 2026-10-13 | **Studies reviewed:** 6
**Publication:** New Scientist | **Section:** New Scientist Mind

---

# Fact-Check Report — New Scientist Mind digest, run date 2026-10-13

---

### Study 1: Most people have intrusive fears of "going crazy" — and OCD makes them stick
**PMID:** 42800306 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

Core numbers check out: N = 154 university students at Memorial University of Newfoundland; 83.1% endorsed at least one psychosis-related intrusion or compulsion; fear of losing control of thoughts/actions most frequently endorsed (50.6%); fear of developing a psychotic illness (18.3%) rated most distressing; 53.2% endorsed replacing "bad thoughts" with better ones; health anxiety and negative beliefs about losing control predicted intrusions over and above OCD severity. The "four in five" gloss is a fair rounding of 83.1%.

**Issue A. Headline and "Why it matters" generalize a student analogue sample to the whole population** — Severity: Moderate

- **As written:** "Most people have intrusive fears of 'going crazy'" / "It suggests that fearing you are going mad is close to a universal human experience rather than a rare symptom"
- **Abstract says:** "This preliminary study examined the prevalence and associated factors of fears of psychosis among a university student sample (N = 154)."
- **Problem:** The Caveats correctly note the population "unlikely to generalize beyond young, educated adults," but the headline and the "Why it matters" line contradict that caveat by extending an 83% figure from one Canadian student convenience sample to "most people" and "a universal human experience." No prevalence claim about the general population is supported here.
- **Suggested fix:** "Most students report intrusive fears of 'going crazy' — and OCD symptoms travel with them" / "It suggests that fearing you are going mad may be a common experience among young adults rather than a rare symptom, and hints that what distinguishes a clinical problem is the meaning attached to losing control."

**Issue B. "OCD makes them stick" asserts causation and persistence the study did not measure** — Severity: Moderate

- **As written:** "and OCD makes them stick" / "what turns it into a clinical problem is not the thought itself but what you believe losing control would mean"
- **Abstract says:** "individuals meeting OCD symptom cut-offs were more likely to endorse psychosis-related fears" and health anxiety and negative beliefs about losing control "predicted psychosis-related unwanted intrusive thoughts" in hierarchical regression.
- **Problem:** This is a cross-sectional questionnaire study with OCD defined by cut-off scores. It shows association, not that OCD causes the thoughts to persist, and nothing about persistence over time was measured. "Turns it into" is likewise causal.
- **Suggested fix:** "...and people with OCD symptoms report them more often" / "...and that beliefs about what losing control would mean are associated with how strongly the fears are endorsed."

**Issue C. Researcher first name not verifiable from the abstract** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "Call Emily Fawcett's group at Memorial University"
- **Abstract says:** "Fawcett EJ ... Electronic address: efawcett@mun.ca" (note two Fawcetts on the byline: Fawcett JM and Fawcett EJ)
- **Problem:** The given name is an inference. Unverifiable from abstract only, and there are two Fawcetts, so a misattribution risk exists.
- **Suggested fix:** "Call senior author E. J. Fawcett at Memorial University (confirm given name before pitching)."

*NS fit:* 6/10 is at the top of what a student analogue sample with self-report measures supports; 5/10 would be safer, and the "first prevalence estimate" claim in the fit note is unverifiable from the abstract (the authors say only "preliminary").

---

### Study 2: People in early psychosis say romance is central to recovery — their clinics almost never ask
**PMID:** 41891676 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

N = 20, early psychosis intervention programs in Ontario, reflexive thematic analysis, Queen's University affiliation, journal and dates all match. Framing is appropriately descriptive and the Caveats are accurate.

**Issue A. "Goal of recovery" slightly recasts the authors' wording** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "Participants described intimacy, romance and sexuality as both a goal of recovery and a yardstick for measuring it"
- **Abstract says:** "Many people experiencing early psychosis see romance, intimacy, and sexuality as facilitators and indicators of recovery"
- **Problem:** "Facilitator" means a contributor to recovery, not a goal of it; the "future goals" sub-theme offers partial support, but the headline construct in the abstract is facilitator/indicator.
- **Suggested fix:** "Participants described intimacy, romance and sexuality as both something that helps recovery along and a yardstick for measuring it."

**Issue B. Unsourced participant quotation and "warnings"** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "Open on a participant describing being told relationships were something to postpone until they were 'stable'." / "when they did, it often came with stipulations or warnings"
- **Abstract says:** "how intimacy, romance, and sexuality are addressed in mental healthcare (e.g., barriers, stipulations, strategies for approaching these topics)"
- **Problem:** "Stipulations" is in the abstract; "warnings" is not. The quoted "stable" scenario appears nowhere in the abstract and reads as if it came from the paper. Unverifiable from abstract only.
- **Suggested fix:** "...and when they did, it often came with stipulations. Pitch angle: open on the theme of clinicians attaching conditions to relationships — ask the authors for an illustrative participant quote from the full text."

*NS fit:* 6/10 is defensible for a well-framed qualitative study, given the digest explicitly says it "can only describe, not quantify."

---

### Study 3: Women's verbal memory advantage vanishes after a first episode of psychosis
**PMID:** 42843653 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

N = 486 across FEP patients, unaffected siblings and controls; RAVLT; rs9896243 in NSF; female C-allele carriers in control and sibling groups outscored males on immediate, short-delay and long-delay recall; advantage absent in FEP; male FEP C-carriers showed the most pronounced recognition deficits. All accurate. Caveats correctly capture the hypothesis-generating functional annotation.

**Issue A. Headline drops the genotype condition and implies a temporal change** — Severity: Moderate

- **As written:** "Women's verbal memory advantage vanishes after a first episode of psychosis"
- **Abstract says:** "Female C-allele carriers in the control and sibling groups showed significantly higher scores... However, this female advantage was not observed in FEP patients."
- **Problem:** Two problems. The advantage reported is specific to C-allele carriers, not women generally; and the design is cross-sectional group comparison, so nothing was observed to change "after" anything — the advantage was simply absent in a different group of people. The body text is accurate, so the headline contradicts it.
- **Suggested fix:** "A memory-linked gene variant favours women — but not women with first-episode psychosis"

**Issue B. "Disappeared entirely" overstates a null result** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "In patients with first-episode psychosis, that female advantage disappeared entirely"
- **Abstract says:** "this female advantage was not observed in FEP patients"
- **Problem:** "Not observed" means the sex difference did not reach significance in that group; "disappeared entirely" asserts a zero effect, which a non-significant finding does not establish.
- **Suggested fix:** "In patients with first-episode psychosis, that female advantage was not seen."

**Issue C. "New mechanism" novelty label overstates what was shown** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "**Novelty:** New mechanism"
- **Abstract says:** Functional annotations "are exploratory and should be considered hypothesis-generating."
- **Problem:** This is a candidate-SNP association with an interaction term, plus in-silico annotation. No mechanism was demonstrated.
- **Suggested fix:** "**Novelty:** Interaction finding / incremental"

*NS fit:* 5/10 is appropriate.

---

### Study 4: Genetic evidence points to clozapine itself driving diabetes risk
**PMID:** 42472444 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

Adelaide University team, Mendelian randomization, higher plasma clozapine and clozapine-norclozapine ratio associated with higher T2D risk and blood pressure, 28 colocalizing markers, 16 with cardiometabolic associations including haematological markers and excretory traits — all accurate. The pitch angle's explicit instruction to avoid implying dose changes is good practice and matches the authors' own caution.

**Issue A. Headline asserts causation the authors explicitly disclaim** — Severity: Moderate

- **As written:** "Genetic evidence points to clozapine itself driving diabetes risk"
- **Abstract says:** "These findings are hypothesis-generating and do not, in the absence of prospective clinical validation, establish causal relationships between clozapine and the identified cardiometabolic traits."
- **Problem:** "Driving" is causal language applied to a finding whose authors state in the conclusions that causation is not established. The body and Caveats hedge correctly, so the headline contradicts the rest of the entry — and a headline is what an editor reads first.
- **Suggested fix:** "Genetic study strengthens the case that clozapine metabolism is tied to diabetes risk"

**Issue B. Ancestry limitation not supported by the abstract** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "relies on existing GWAS summary data whose ancestry composition limits generalizability"
- **Abstract says:** Nothing about data sources, cohorts or ancestry composition.
- **Problem:** Plausible for MR work, but unverifiable from abstract only. Stating it as fact in the Caveats invites a correction if the underlying GWAS are more diverse than assumed.
- **Suggested fix:** "relies on genetic summary data; check the source cohorts' ancestry composition before pitching generalizability claims."

*NS fit:* 5/10 is well judged for a hypothesis-generating pipeline. Note the abstract carries no funding or competing-interest statement, so nothing to flag as omitted.

---

### Study 5: There may be no single recipe for recovering from schizophrenia
**PMID:** 42734987 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

N = 101 with schizophrenia or schizoaffective disorder; finite mixture regression; three-class solution with one class too small to interpret; one class associated with social functioning, depressive symptoms, positive symptoms and metacognition; the other showing no single dominant predictor despite similar symptom and functioning levels; negative symptoms associated in both larger classes. All accurate, and the Caveats are unusually thorough. Headline is appropriately hedged ("may be").

**Issue A. "Overturns prior research" misstates the contribution** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "**Novelty:** Overturns prior research"
- **Abstract says:** "findings regarding the strength and direction of these associations have been inconsistent, suggesting that different association structures may exist within the population... one class... reflect[s] a multidimensional association pattern consistent with previous findings."
- **Problem:** The study reconciles inconsistent prior findings rather than overturning them, and one class explicitly replicates the existing literature.
- **Suggested fix:** "**Novelty:** Reframes existing findings"

**Issue B. "Whether life feels worth living" glosses a defined construct** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "for whom completely different things determine whether life feels worth living"
- **Abstract says:** "Personal recovery was treated as the dependent variable."
- **Problem:** Personal recovery is a specific measured construct (hope, identity, meaning, empowerment, depending on instrument), not a global judgement about life's worth. "Determine" also imports causation into a cross-sectional association, which the Caveats correctly disclaim.
- **Suggested fix:** "for whom completely different factors are associated with how far they feel they are personally recovering."

*NS fit:* 5/10 is defensible; the digest names the data-hungriness of mixture modelling at N = 101 itself.

---

### Study 6: Two ways reality can go wrong: the philosopher's case for comparing borderline and schizophrenia
**PMID:** 42853770 | **Verdict:** ✅ Accurate

No factual errors found. Framing is consistent with the abstract. "Evanescence of reality," "excess of reality," "ontic gravity," the oblique-versus-direct gaze contrast and the epoché framing all match the source, the entry states plainly that this is conceptual work with no data, the pitch angle instructs the writer to be explicit that it is theory, and the 4/10 fit score is appropriate for a non-empirical paper.

---

**Total issues:** 12 (8 Minor, 4 Moderate, 0 Major)
**Entries requiring revision:** 5

**Cross-cutting note:** The recurring pattern is headlines running ahead of accurate body text and Caveats — studies 1, 3 and 4 all carry correct hedging in the entry but causal or overgeneralized headlines. Fixing the six headline lines would resolve all four Moderate issues. No NS fit score is 7 or above, and none rests on evidence weaker than the score implies, though study 1 would sit more comfortably at 5/10.
